finding.text: `insert_at()` (Recite.js, new method after `queue()`) treats `chunks[0]`'s run as "the one playing", but played chunks stay in `chunks` until `stop()`/`cancel_unheard()` (Recite.js:254 `finish()` leaves them; the new stale test itself says so). From the third reply of a session on, a new reply lands among already-heard chunks and `this.at` is never shifted. Example: chunks [R1 heard, R2 playing at 1], new X inserts at 1 → `at` now points at X, then `ended()` plays index 2 = R2 again. When idle after `finish()` (chunks [R1, R2] both heard), X goes in at 1, plays, then R2 is read a second time. The anchor must be the run around `this.at` (or `wait_at` while held), and an idle queue with nothing waiting should append at the end; add a test that queues three replies one after another, letting each finish.

Rule 3 ("held updates keep their behaviour") is broken, and the outcome says "untouched". `final()` then `flush_updates()` (Recite.js:274, :281) queue the direct answer D and then each held update through `queue_update()` → `queue()`, and every fresh reply now goes right after the front. While something is playing, the order becomes [playing, U2, U1, D]: the updates jump ahead of the direct answer they were held behind, and they come out in reverse order. Held updates (and `queue_update`) need to be queued behind D, for example with an "append" flag on `queue()`. There also needs to be a test of an update held while a reply plays.

Comments that no longer match the code: `queue_update`'s doc still says "behind whatever is already queued" (Recite.js:452), and `flush_updates`'s doc still says "in the order they arrived, behind … the direct answer" (Recite.js:458). The readme's no-flood paragraph (readme.md, "No flood") still promises the direct answer plays ahead of held updates. Each should be updated once finding 2 is fixed.

`skip_stale()` runs only from `ended()`. A stale reply that sits at `wait_at` (turn-taking hold) or is started by `start_or_hold()` after an idle gap is still read late. That is fine under the "only if tiny" rule, but the readme says flatly "is skipped, not read late".

The tests (`Recite.order.test.mjs`) always start from an empty `chunks` array, so the stale-chunk anchor in finding 1 is never exercised. The scenario test asserts `r.at` indices, which would stay green even if the wrong text played.

A streamed reply never plays newest-first, and streaming is the smart reply's normal path. `partial()` gives a new stream `live.id` (Recite.js:393), and `take()` queues its first sentence as a continuation. `insert_at()` then finds no chunk with that id and returns `chunks.length` (Recite.js `insert_at`, "the first chunk of a fresh stream"). So a new streamed reply lands behind replies A and B that are already waiting, which is the reverse of what the brief asks. The first chunk of a stream should use the fresh-reply anchor. Test 4 in `Recite.order.test.mjs` passes only because nothing was waiting when its stream began.

When a continuation lands at or before `this.at`, `queue()` doesn't shift `this.at`. It does shift `wait_at` and `pending_ids` (Recite.js `queue()`, the splice line). Example: stream S plays S1. An agent update U arrives and is appended (no cue is pending mid-stream). S1 ends and U starts at index 1. Then S2 streams in and goes to index 1, right after S's run. `at` now points at S2 while U's audio plays, so `ended()` plays index 2, which is U again. S2 is never read. The old tail-append code did not have this bug. Fix: shift `this.at` (when playing or paused) whenever `at <= this.at`, or append a continuation whose run has already finished. Add a test for it.

A reply held for quiet (`wait_at`, never started) anchors fresh replies behind it (`insert_at`: `this.wait_at ?? this.at`). So the older held reply still plays before a newer one, while rule 1 says "not yet started" replies yield to the newest. The choice is defensible, but neither the readme nor the task log records it as a decision with its alternative.

`skip_stale()` can cut a reply that is already playing, which breaks rule 1 ("a reply already playing is never cut"). It is called from `ended()` with `at + 1` (worktree/qf-2 Recite.js:291, :297), and it checks only `chunks[i].ts`, never whether `chunks[i].reply` is the reply now playing. Every sentence of a reply carries the timestamp of the moment it was queued, so a long reply that takes more than 2 minutes to read, or one that is paused by barge-in and resumed more than 2 minutes later, loses the rest of its sentences at the next sentence boundary. Fix: stop at `chunks[i].reply === chunks[this.at].reply` (only skip runs that have never started), and add a test that ages a playing reply's second sentence.

`skip_stale()`'s `pending_ids` remap handles only `p.last === end` (marked played) and `p.last > end` (shifted). An entry whose `last` falls inside the dropped run but is not its end keeps an index that now points at another reply (Recite.js:302). This is rare, because `last` is normally the run's end, but `p.last >= i && p.last <= end` is the safer test.

`skip_stale()` calls `Recite.mark_played()` for a dropped reply but never calls `recite.on_read` with `heard: "skipped"`, which `cancel_unheard()` does (readme.md, "Cutting-in settings"). So a page can't tell that a stale reply was dropped rather than heard. That's fine under "only if tiny", but it should be wired up if `on_read` ever gets a consumer.
